posts.name: want-vs-enjoy

reel.closing: Your brain can learn the other way.

posts.caption:
Why is p*rn so hard to quit, even when you don't enjoy it much anymore?

Researchers have found that "wanting" and "liking" run on different systems in the brain. With repetition, the wanting can grow very loud while the actual enjoyment stays small. That's why the urge promises so much and delivers so little.

It's not a character flaw. It's a learned pattern, and patterns can be unlearned, one urge at a time. 🧠

(Source: Berridge & Robinson's incentive-salience research)

Save this for a hard night.

That's what Guardian does: a calm curtain over p*rn sites, so you get a moment to choose. Follow to know when it launches. 🛡️

posts.name: urge-plan

reel.closing: Save this for the next urge.

posts.caption:
Your 3-step plan for the next time the urge to watch p*rn hits:

1. Leave the room. Change the setting and you break the script.
2. Move. Push-ups, a walk, cold water. Give the energy somewhere to go.
3. Breathe. In for 4, hold for 7, out for 8. Repeat four times.

Decide now, so you don't have to decide in the moment. Save this and use it tonight. 📌

posts.name: not-a-bad-person

lines.emphasis: doesn't make you a bad person.

reel.closing: Send this to someone who needs it.

posts.caption:
If you're struggling to quit p*rn, read this twice: it doesn't make you a bad person.

Shame is what keeps the cycle going. You slip, you feel worthless, and that feeling is exactly what drives you back to it. Honesty breaks the loop: admitting it, talking about it, getting back up without punishing yourself.

You're not broken. You're fighting. Send this to someone who needs to hear it. 💜

posts.name: the-real-thing
posts.caption:
P*rn is staged, edited and scripted. And the screen never shows whether the person in it actually chose to be there.

Real connection is slower, more awkward, and far better: real people, on real terms.

That's what you're fighting for. Tag someone who's choosing the real thing too. 💜
